prompt.context: A hospital group has been experiencing growing pains and has asked our firm for help.
prompt.question: The hospital group originally consisted of one hospital and then acquired 3 other hospitals. Its profits are going down. Identify the root cause of the profitability decline and recommend a course of action.

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by growing pains?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital group originally consisted of one hospital and then it acquired 3 other hospitals, and its profits are going down.
Yes, the CEO of the main hospital changed; it was originally an MD doctor, now it is a business experience MBA.

clarifying_info.q: Any other changes or events impacting the hospital group?
What are the revenue streams for the hospital?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital treats patients and mainly collects payments from the insurance companies based on the service provided.

clarifying_info.q: Has the volume of patients changed?
Has there been any change in mix of services performed by the hospital (lower number of surgeries etc.)?
Can you explain the insurance coverage categories?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily the patients can be categorized into: Private Insurance Covered Patients, Public Insurance Covered Patients, and No Insurance Covered Patients (usually homeless people). Payments from private insurance are greater than public insurance.

clarifying_info.q: What drives patients with private insurance to the hospital?
What is the price of the billing outsourcing service to physicians?
What is the physician annual profit?
How does the physician spend their time?
clarifying_info.a: 75% on patient care, 15% on billing, 10% on administrative overhead.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue of the doctor's office?
Does the physician incur additional cost when adding 15% additional patient care time?

exhibits.title: Physician Survey Results
exhibits.shows: Survey results from physicians who normally refer patients to the hospital, showing their sentiments or ratings about the hospital after the management change
exhibits.data: Survey data on physician perception/satisfaction (majority indifferent about the hospital)

exhibits.title: Physician Survey Results (continued)
exhibits.shows: Additional survey data from physicians, highlighting key issues they face when dealing with the hospital
exhibits.data: Survey data indicating complex billing as a major issue for physicians

framework: Identify whether the profitability decline is in the main hospital or the acquired hospitals
Decompose profitability into revenue and costs for the main hospital
Explore revenue drivers: volume of patients, mix of services, revenue per patient (patient insurance mix)
Identify that patient mix has shifted toward lower-reimbursing insurance (fewer private insurance patients)
Identify the driver of private insurance patients: physician referrals
Hypothesize that management change has affected physician perception and thus referrals
Test the hypothesis via physician survey
Identify actionable solutions to rebuild physician relationships (e.g., billing outsourcing service)
Perform cost-benefit analysis of the billing outsourcing service for physicians

questions.prompt: The acquired hospitals did not experience any decline in profits. What does this tell you, and what is your next step?
questions.guidance: The candidate should quickly focus on the main hospital as the source of profitability decline and stop attributing the problem to the acquisition. Next step: decompose profit of the main hospital into revenue and costs.

questions.prompt: Costs for the main hospital have not changed. Revenue has declined. What is driving the revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should explore revenue = volume × price per patient. Volume has not changed and service mix has not changed, so revenue per patient (on average) must be falling. This implies the patient mix in terms of insurance coverage is shifting — fewer high-paying private insurance patients and more public/uninsured patients.

questions.prompt: What hypothesis would you form about why fewer private-insurance patients are coming to the main hospital?
questions.guidance: Because private-insurance patients are referred by private physicians, a decline in private-insurance volume implies fewer physician referrals. The likely driver is that the management change (MD to MBA CEO) changed physician perception of the hospital, leading to fewer referrals.

questions.prompt: How would you test this hypothesis?
questions.guidance: Conduct a survey of physicians who normally refer patients to the hospital, asking about their satisfaction, perception of hospital management, and any specific issues they face.

questions.prompt: Review Exhibits 1 and 2 — the physician survey results. What are the key insights?
questions.guidance: Majority of doctors are indifferent about the hospital, which is not good for referrals. One major issue physicians cite is complex billing. The candidate should identify that improving physician relationships and addressing billing complexity are priorities.

questions.prompt: The hospital has a billing outsourcing service it does not aggressively market to physicians. How would you judge whether this is a viable service for physicians? Calculate the ROI, new profit, and increase in profit percentage.
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize that if a physician outsources billing, the 15% of time previously spent on billing can be redirected to patient care. Since no additional cost is incurred, this generates new revenue. The candidate should ask for physician revenue before calculating. Layout: Revenue earned if billing outsourced = 425,000 × (15%/75%). Then compare benefit vs. cost of outsourcing.

math.setup: Physician Revenue = $425,000; Physician Profit = $175,000; Physician Cost = $250,000. Time allocation: 75% patient care, 15% billing, 10% admin. If billing outsourced: 15% time freed = additional 15%/75% = 20% more patient care time. Cost of outsourcing service = $50,000. No additional operating costs incurred.
math.answer: ROI = 70%; New Profit = $210,000; Increase in Profit = 20%

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential actions the hospital can take to strengthen relationships with private physicians and reverse the decline in private-insurance patient referrals?

categories.name: Physician Relationship Building
ideas: Host regular physician engagement events and dinners
Create a physician advisory board to involve MDs in hospital decisions
Assign relationship managers to key referring physicians
Provide regular hospital performance updates to physician partners

categories.name: Billing Outsourcing Service
ideas: Aggressively market the billing outsourcing service to physicians
Offer introductory pricing or a pilot period
Demonstrate ROI of 70% and 20% profit increase through case studies
Bundle billing service with other administrative support offerings

categories.name: Operational Improvements
ideas: Simplify the billing and administrative processes for physicians
Improve turnaround times on referral scheduling
Upgrade communication channels between hospital and referring physicians
Streamline credentialing and onboarding for new referring physicians

categories.name: Management & Culture
ideas: Have the new CEO personally meet with top referring physicians
Reinforce clinical quality messaging to physicians
Establish an MD liaison role bridging management and physician community
Conduct ongoing physician satisfaction surveys to track improvements

recommendation: The hospital group's profitability decline is driven by the main hospital's revenue decline, caused by a shift in patient mix toward lower-reimbursing insurance patients due to fewer referrals from private physicians. This is likely a consequence of the management change from an MD to an MBA CEO, which has altered physician perception and reduced referral motivation.

To reverse the decline, the hospital should aggressively market its billing outsourcing service to private physicians. This service delivers a 70% ROI within one year and increases physician profits by 20%, providing a compelling value proposition that rebuilds the relationship with referring physicians and incentivizes them to send more private-insurance patients.
risks: Physicians may remain indifferent even after outreach if trust in management is not rebuilt
Competitors may offer similar or better billing solutions
The billing outsourcing service may not be scalable to serve all physician partners simultaneously
Revenue recovery may take time even if referral relationships improve
next_steps: Conduct a targeted outreach campaign to the top referring physicians led by senior leadership
Launch a formal marketing push for the billing outsourcing service with a demonstrated ROI case study
Implement a physician satisfaction tracking mechanism to monitor relationship recovery
Assess whether the new CEO should bring on MD advisors or a Chief Medical Officer to restore physician confidence
